faq.a: Four directions: JSON → CSV, CSV → JSON, JSON → Markdown table, and JSON → SQL INSERT statements (with a configurable table name). The JSON side expects an array of objects (a single object is wrapped into one). A live preview table shows up to the first 50 rows before you copy or download.

faq.q: How are nested objects and arrays handled?
faq.a: Nested objects are flattened with a configurable separator (default '.'), so {"user":{"name":"John"}} becomes a 'user.name' column — and you can cap the flatten depth at 1–3 levels or leave it unlimited. For arrays you choose: join into one cell (with a custom delimiter), expand to numbered columns, or explode into multiple rows. Arrays of objects are the hard case, so check the row count against your record count.

faq.q: Can I control the CSV delimiter, quoting and encoding?
faq.a: Yes. Delimiter can be comma, semicolon, tab or pipe; line endings LF or CRLF; you can quote all fields; set how null is written; and the header row is optional. For CSV → JSON there's auto-delimiter detection, a 'first row is header' toggle, type inference (numbers/booleans/null), and pretty or minified output. The parser follows RFC 4180 — quoted fields may contain commas and newlines.

faq.q: Can it handle large files without freezing?
faq.a: The JSON → CSV path converts in 500-row chunks with a live row counter so the page stays responsive, and shows input/output byte sizes with a percentage change. The 'ZIP (+ split)' export bundles your input, the full converted output, and — when the result exceeds 1000 rows — splits it into numbered part files inside a chunks/ folder, plus a README. CSV exports include a UTF-8 BOM so Hindi/Devanagari opens correctly in Excel.
